articleSummary: Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, issued a sanitary alert for herbivore rabies in São Francisco de Paula (Serra Gaúcha) and Caraá (Litoral Norte), with risk to Canela, Três Coroas, Riozinho, Maquiné, and Rolante (Vale do Paranhana). In 2026, at least 45 active foci have been identified across ten regions, underscoring a preventive vaccination strategy to protect cattle, buffalo, horses, sheep, and pigs. Wilson Hoffmeister of Seapi notes several foci persist from last year, making rapid vaccination and reporting refuges essential for field teams. Rabies in herbivores is mainly transmitted by Desmodus rotundus, the vampire bat; human exposure can occur via saliva. Guidelines call for annual inactivated-vaccine immunization for all livestock, roost monitoring, and targeted bat-control by official defense agencies. Notifiable signs: suspected animals with choking or bite-mark indications; do not open mouths. The disease progresses from behavioral changes to progressive neurological symptoms and fatal paralysis within 3–7 days.

articleSummary: Hantavirus is a zoonotic disease that has drawn attention in Indonesia and worldwide, but experts say it is unlikely to cause a Covid-like pandemic. Transmission is rodent-related: humans acquire infection by inhaling dust contaminated with virus particles from the urine, saliva, or feces of infected rodents, not via direct person-to-person spread. Global data from BKPK of the Ministry of Health note hantavirus cases in various regions, with two main groups producing different health impacts. In Indonesia, high-risk groups include sanitation workers, waste handlers, farmers, and laboratory animal workers. Prevention centers on breaking rodent–human contact: keep homes clean to deter rodent nests, use PPE (masks and gloves) when cleaning contaminated areas, and store food securely. Symptoms such as high fever, severe headache, nausea, or diarrhea after exposure warrant prompt medical evaluation.

articleSummary: Malaria (Plasmodium spp.) remains a global threat; China eliminated local transmission in 2021, but imported cases persist year-round due to cross-border travel, with border areas as a priority. Five human-infecting Plasmodium species exist: P. falciparum (most virulent), P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale, and P. knowlesi. Cure is achievable with early diagnosis and full, supervised treatment. Prevention includes pre-travel consultation, protective measures, vector control, and, if advised, chemoprophylaxis. After returning, monitor for 1 year and seek prompt testing if febrile, informing travel history. Blood donation deferral applies to recent travel to endemic areas or malaria recovery within 3 years.

articleSummary: Global health authorities should monitor free-living amoebae, particularly Naegleria fowleri, as climate change and aging water infrastructure may accelerate spread. A study, The Rising Threat of Amoebae: A Global Public Health Challenge, published in Biocontaminant by Shenyang Agricultural University, links warming waters and inadequate water management to wider distribution of these amoebae in rivers, lakes, soils, and water distribution systems. While most amoebae are harmless, N. fowleri can invade nasal passages during recreational water use and cause fatal primary amoebic meningoencephalitis. The amoebae can host bacteria and viruses inside themselves, enabling survival against disinfection—a Trojan horse effect that could sustain pathogens and potentially drive antibiotic resistance. Researchers advocate One Health approaches, improved surveillance, rapid diagnostics, and advanced water-treatment tools to curb emerging threats across regions.

Across both countries, 25 recoveries and 6,525 contacts are under follow-up; 34 healthcare workers infected (29 in DRC, 5 in Uganda). The Africa CDC Advisory and Technical Council (ATC) urges stronger community engagement, cross-border cooperation, and enhanced frontline response amid insecurity and misinformation. Priorities include expanding laboratory capacity with molecular diagnostics and rapid tests; improving case investigation, contact tracing, laboratory confirmation, isolation, clinical care, and infection prevention; One Health surveillance; readiness in non-affected areas; and better humanitarian access and civil–military coordination. articleSummary: As of 13 June 2026, the Democratic Republic of Congo reports 689 confirmed Ebola cases and 139 deaths, with 17 new cases and 5 deaths recorded on Thursday. Transmission is active in Ituri, North Kivu, and South Kivu; 168 suspected cases and 64 deaths are under investigation. Containment is hindered by limited Ebola treatment facilities, shortages of supplies, and funding gaps. The outbreak is driven by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, a rare strain with no approved specific treatment or vaccine; other strains include Sudan, Tai Forest, Reston, Bombali, and Zaire. Past outbreaks include West Africa’s 2014–2016 epidemic (>28,000 cases), Congo’s 1976 first identification of Ebola, last year’s Congo outbreak with 34 deaths, and the 2018–2020 period (~2,300 deaths). Transmission occurs via blood and body fluids; animals such as monkeys, apes, porcupines, and pigs can harbor the virus. Symptoms appear 2–21 days after exposure, starting with fever, headache, and muscle pains, potentially progressing to vomiting, rash, and bleeding. Prevention focuses on avoiding bushmeat, properly cooking meat, isolation, contact tracing, and supportive care.

articleHeadline: Kerala's zoonotic potential in the background of Nipah
articleSummary: NiV recurs in Kerala with a 2018 outbreak of 23 cases (18 lab-confirmed), CFR 91% and two survivors. Subsequent spillovers include 2019 Ernakulam single case (survived), 2021 Malappuram 12-year-old, 2023 Kozhikode cluster of six, and 2024 two single cases from Malappuram (July and September). In 2025, four Nipah cases occurred in Malappuram and Palakkad with no epidemiological links, indicating independent spillovers from the natural reservoir. Kerala’s vulnerability stems from ecological-demographic-climatic convergence along the Western Ghats and dense human-wildlife interfaces; WHO lists Nipah as a priority pathogen, prompting enhanced surveillance and infection-control measures.

articleSummary: Oviedo, 13 June 2026 — At the 32nd National Congress of Spain's General and Family Physicians (SEMG), experts analyzed emerging viruses and identified misinformation as a major global health weakness. In Europe, hantavirus risk is currently low; most cases are zoonotic from rodents, with human-to-human transmission rare and requiring close contact. articleSummary: Brazil's Ministry of Health has temporarily suspended the Butantan dengue vaccine after 42 alarm-symptom cases among recipients, including three hospitalizations and two deaths under investigation. articleHeadline: Why 'brain-eating amoeba' cases are seeing surge in Kerala: 'Tropical climate, poor water quality inducing growth'
articleSummary: Kerala, India, is experiencing a surge in amoebic meningoencephalitis driven by Acanthamoeba, causing granulomatous amoebic encephalitis (GAE). In the first five months of 2026, 133 positive cases and 33 deaths have been reported. While primary amoebic meningitis (PAM) caused by Naegleria fowleri has declined, most detections are GAE. Since 2016, Kerala previously averaged few cases (eight until 2023) but recorded 36 cases with nine deaths in 2024 and 201;47 deaths in 2025; by June 12, 2026, 133 cases and 33 deaths. The spike follows rigorous testing of all unidentified encephalitis cases and a 2024 treatment protocol that improved early detection and reduced mortality. The first Indian PAM survivor was a 14-year-old in 2024. Contributing factors include tropical climate and poor water quality, with vegetation in water bodies and high coliform counts; many households have toilet pits near open wells. Most affected are elderly or immunocompromised.
notes: Acanthamoeba による肉芽腫性アメーバ脳炎（GAE）の急激な増加が主題。2024年の治療プロトコール導入により早期発見と死亡率低下が実現したにもかかわらず、症例数が爆発的に増加している点が重要。水質汚濁、熱帯気候、衛生インフラ不足が根本要因として指摘されており、持続的な曝露リスクが高い。高齢者と免疫不全者が主要な被害グループであることから、脆弱集団への甚大な影響が懸念される。

articleHeadline: The hunt for a new Ebola vaccine
articleSummary: Outbreak of Bundibugyo Ebola virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda has over 350 confirmed cases and dozens of deaths; no vaccine approved for Bundibugyo. Oxford researchers Teresa Lambe and Rebecca Makinson are developing a vaccine, with early June 2026 funding from CEPI. Bundibugyo, first identified in 2007 in western Uganda, is a zoonotic filovirus with fruit bats suspected as natural reservoirs. While related to Zaire Ebola, Bundibugyo’s glycoprotein amino acid sequence is about 60% similar, limiting confidence that vaccines targeting Zaire would protect against Bundibugyo. Two vaccines licensed for Zaire exist: Ervebo (single-shot) and Zabdeno/Mvabea (two-shot), both viral-vector vaccines delivering Ebola glycoprotein. The main hurdles are funding and logistics; outbreaks affect relatively few people but have high fatality and occur where healthcare infrastructure is weak, complicating manufacturing, transport, storage, and rapid immunization. The article notes limited cross-protection data and ongoing research.

articleSummary: Vaccine-derived poliovirus type-1 (VDPV-1) detected in Ghaziabad sewage triggers an eradication blueprint. Ghaziabad, in Western Uttar Pradesh, has been allocated 9.32 lakh polio doses from the Meerut division; nine districts together receive 54.16 lakh doses and 2.78 lakh vials. A stringent cold chain is being established with a nodal officer and assurances of uninterrupted electricity to the district e-vaccine stores, plus new ice-pack boxes and cold-chain vans. More than 6,000 vaccination teams will participate as the polio campaign begins on 28 June, targeting over seven lakh children in Ghaziabad and aiming to vaccinate all children under five. Some districts have already collected vaccines; the Joint Director of the Meerut division, Dr. Ashok Talian, confirmed allocations.
